questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x+{y}^{2},\,y(0)=3
$$

Using the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx=0.25,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step.
Which of the following is the **general form** of $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ in terms of the new values ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and the current value $y?$
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In general $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =({x}_{\text{new}}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 0.25 \\  & =0.25\,{x}_{\text{new}}+0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side to define $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.25\,{x}_{\text{new}}+0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{2} \\ {{-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-0.25\,{x}_{\text{new}}}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.25$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=-0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-0.25\,{x}_{\text{new}}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={y}^{3}-x,\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step.
Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}}\cdot 1 \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}} \\ {{{y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.$ Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-1+2 \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,y(0)=1
$$

Use the implicit Euler method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(0.5).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(0.5)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0.5,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0.5-0=0.5.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.5$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5{x}_{\text{new}}({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-0.5({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+0.5=0.5.$ Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5(0.5)({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1-0.5(0.5)^{2} \\  & =0.25({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.125.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method. 

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.25(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-1.125}{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})+1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈0.916667 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈0.915476 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈0.915476\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(0.5)≈0.92,$ rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-2}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0.5)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.2 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.179747 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.179509\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1)≈1.18,$ rounded to two decimal places.

questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,{y}_{0}=y({x}_{0}),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=0.9,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=0.9-0.4=0.5.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(2({x}_{\text{new}})-({y}_{\text{new}})^{2})\cdot 0.5 \\  & =({x}_{\text{new}})-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g({y}_{\text{new}}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+({x}_{\text{new}})-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-({x}_{\text{new}})=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=0.5$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-y-({x}_{\text{new}}).
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is ${x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0.4+0.5=0.9.$ Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-1.2-(0.9) \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+{y}_{\text{new}}-2.1.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1.2$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method. 

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-2.1}{({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}+1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(0.4)=1.2,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1.2 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & =1.281818 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.280351 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.280351\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = y^3 - x\,y, \qquad y(1)=1
$$

Using the implicit Euler method with step size $\Delta x = 1,$ the new value $y_\text{new}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g(y_\text{new}) = 0$ at each step.
Which of the following is the **specific function** $g(y_\text{new})$ used in the first step?

- $g(y_\text{new}) = (y_\text{new})^3 - 3y_\text{new} - 1$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = 3y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^3 + 1$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = 3y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^3 - 1$

- $g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^3 + x_\text{new}y_\text{new}$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y_0 = y(x_0),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta y = y'_\text{new} \cdot \Delta x,
$$

with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In general, $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}} \\  & =({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g(y_\text{new}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {{{y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}}-y}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $\Delta x = 1$ is

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = y_\text{new} - (y_\text{new})^3 + x_\text{new}y_\text{new} - y.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 1 + 1 = 2.$ Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+2{y}_{\text{new}}-1 \\  & =3{y}_{\text{new}}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 2xy + y^3, \qquad y(1.5)=-0.3
$$

Use the implicit Euler method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(2).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y_0 = y(x_0),
$$

the implicit Euler method with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\Delta y = y'_\text{new} \cdot \Delta x,
$$

with $y'_\text{new} = f(x_\text{new},y_\text{new})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
\Delta x = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the implicit Euler method. In general, $\Delta y$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & ={y}_{\text{new}}^{′}\cdot Δx \\  & =(2{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{3})\cdot 0.5 \\  & ={x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y$ and move all terms to the left-hand side and define the resulting expression as $g(y_\text{new}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+{x}_{\text{new}}{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
0.5(y_\text{new})^3 + (x_\text{new}-1)y_\text{new} + y = 0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $\Delta x = 0.5$ is

$$
g(y_\text{new}) = 0.5(y_\text{new})^3 + (x_\text{new}-1)y_\text{new} + y.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.$ The old $y$ value is $y = -0.3.$ Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+(2-1){y}_{\text{new}}-0.3 \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-0.3.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=-0.3$ to solve $g(y_\text{new}) = 0.$ We'll use Newton's method. 

$$
(y_\text{new})_{n+1} = (y_\text{new})_n - \dfrac{g(y_\text{new})}{g'(y_\text{new})}
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
g'(y_\text{new}) = 1.5(y_\text{new})^2 + 1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
(y_\text{new})_{n+1} = (y_\text{new})_n - \dfrac{0.5((y_\text{new})_n)^3 + (y_\text{new})_n - 0.3}{1.5((y_\text{new})_n)^2 + 1}
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(1.5) = -0.3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =-0.3 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈0.240529 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈0.288849 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈0.288050\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2) \approx 0.29,$ rounded to two decimal places.
